purpose: Original low-stakes English diagnostic and practice tasks. Level labels describe curriculum design targets, not empirically calibrated item difficulties or CEFR cut scores.
limitations: The 100 original diagnostic items include reading, actual-audio listening scripts, controlled form checks, open writing and real speaking across A1-C1. None is unit-mastery evidence.
Listening scripts require actual audio delivery with the transcript hidden. The repository provides original scripts, not licensed human recordings or acoustic validation.
Each stimulus family supplies at most one independent diagnostic trial; prompted, revealed, repeated and transcript-visible trials cannot create new diagnostic evidence.
Open production may be reviewed by an LLM for provisional feedback. Only genuine human reviews enter confirmed productive evidence; identity is not authenticated.
No item calibration, standard-setting, rater reliability or outcome validation study has established CEFR measurement properties. Provisional routing is not mastery or certification.

items.prompt: How did volunteering affect Elena's plans?
options: She concluded that customers did not want recommendations.
She decided to gain relevant work experience before opening a shop.
She abandoned her interest in selling books.
She decided to invest her savings immediately.
answers: She decided to gain relevant work experience before opening a shop.
items.context: Elena had always wanted to run a small bookshop. When the town library invited volunteers to organise a weekend book exchange, she signed up. She enjoyed recommending books, but dealing with boxes, prices and schedules was less enjoyable. The experience did not end her ambition. It persuaded her to work in a shop first, so that she could learn the practical side before investing her savings.

items.prompt: What has the manager decided?

To open early every day permanently.
To end all morning sessions.
To hire extra afternoon staff immediately.
answers: To continue the experiment on a limited schedule.
items.context: The sports centre tested an earlier opening time for a month. Morning attendance rose, especially among people starting work at nine. However, the centre needed an extra member of staff, and afternoon attendance fell slightly. The manager will keep the early opening for two days a week while collecting more information. A permanent daily change has not been agreed.

To replace the hall's entrance.

answers: To find a compromise between funding repairs and limiting advertising.
items.context: A local company offered to repair the village hall for free, provided that its logo could appear above the entrance for five years. Some residents welcomed the offer because the roof urgently needed attention. Others felt that the building should not become an advertisement. The committee has asked the company whether a smaller sign inside the hall would be acceptable.

items.prompt: What helped Sam manage his study time?
options: Receiving answers from classmates.

Regular planning discussions with classmates.

answers: Regular planning discussions with classmates.
items.context: Sam joined an online course because he could study after his children went to bed. He liked the recorded explanations and the ability to repeat difficult sections. Sam now finishes most tasks earlier, although the course content has not changed.

items.prompt: What changed the speaker's experience of audiobooks?

answers: Listening to a sample before choosing.

delivery.text: I used to choose audiobooks just because I liked the author. A few disappointed me, even though I had enjoyed the printed books. Then a friend suggested listening to a sample before buying. I discovered that the narrator's voice and pace mattered a lot to me. I still listen to long novels, but now I check who is reading them first.

items.prompt: Why did the speaker prefer the new cleaning arrangement?

Now each of us has one shared area to clean each week, and we swap areas on Sunday. The work takes just as long, but at least we know what we have agreed to do.

options: The increase in trade cannot confidently be attributed to the cycle lane alone.
The cycle lane definitely caused the entire increase in trade.
All nearby shops experienced the same change in sales.
Seasonal demand has been ruled out as an explanation.
answers: The increase in trade cannot confidently be attributed to the cycle lane alone.
items.context: A council report credits a new cycle lane with increasing local trade. Shopkeepers interviewed near the lane described busier weekends, and card payments in the area rose. However, the report compares this spring with the previous winter, when several streets were closed for repairs. It also excludes nearby streets without a cycle lane. The change may have helped businesses, but the evidence does not isolate its effect from seasonal demand or the end of the roadworks.

items.prompt: Why is the company reviewing its interviews?
options: Anonymous applications made the shortlist less varied.
Applicants have refused to attend interviews.
University names are required to evaluate interview answers.
Changes at the initial stage have not resolved the whole recruitment problem.
answers: Changes at the initial stage have not resolved the whole recruitment problem.
items.context: An employer introduced anonymous applications to reduce bias in initial recruitment. Applicants' names and university names were removed before shortlisting. The shortlist became more varied, but the final hiring pattern changed little. The company now plans to review interview questions and panel training as well. Its director described anonymous applications as a useful first step rather than a complete solution.

items.prompt: What do the organisers value about refusing some repairs?
options: It allows volunteers to avoid explaining their decisions.
It proves that most household objects are unsafe.
It can demonstrate responsible judgment and strengthen trust.
It guarantees that visitors will buy replacements.
answers: It can demonstrate responsible judgment and strengthen trust.
items.context: The city's repair café is often presented as a way to save money. Volunteers say that this is only part of its appeal. Visitors learn how ordinary objects work, meet neighbours and sometimes discover that an item cannot be repaired safely. Rather than promising to fix everything, the café explains the limits of repairs. The organisers believe that an honest refusal can build more trust than an unsuccessful attempt to please every visitor.

items.prompt: What is the purpose of the next trial's design?
options: To prove the first trial's conclusion without collecting more data.
To separate the workshop's effect from differences in who chooses to attend.
To ensure that only highly motivated students receive invitations.
To compare assignment topics rather than completion behaviour.
answers: To separate the workshop's effect from differences in who chooses to attend.
items.context: A university trial offered students an optional weekly planning workshop. Participants submitted more assignments on time than non-participants. The organisers would like to expand the scheme, but students who volunteered may already have been more motivated. The next trial will allocate invitations randomly and compare results across similar courses. The researchers want to establish whether the workshop changes behaviour, rather than merely attracting students likely to do well.

items.prompt: What mainly disappointed the speaker about the flexible rail pass?
options: The price was higher than the advertised price.
The practical restrictions conflicted with the promise of spontaneity.
The routes excluded the places the speaker wanted to visit.
The trains took longer than the timetable suggested.
answers: The practical restrictions conflicted with the promise of spontaneity.

delivery.text: The rail pass was advertised as a way to make plans as you travelled. It did cover the routes I wanted, and the price was reasonable. What I had not understood was that seats on several useful trains had to be reserved days ahead. I do not object to reservations in principle. I object to selling the pass as freedom to decide on the morning, when that was not realistic for much of my route.

items.prompt: Why does the speaker favour delaying the release?
options: To add the optional features requested by the largest customer.
To avoid publishing the results of an unfinished trial.
To make the existing core function dependable before expansion.
To replace the original product with a different design.
answers: To make the existing core function dependable before expansion.

delivery.text: I am not asking for another month so that we can add more features. We have already postponed the optional ones, which was sensible. But the main function still fails when several people use it at once. Launching now would mean asking customers to rely on something we know is unreliable. A narrower product that works is worth releasing; the current version is narrow without yet being dependable.

items.prompt: How has the speaker's view of the translation changed?
options: The speaker now prefers the smoother version for its speed.
The speaker now sees the awkward wording as evidence of careless editing.
The speaker now thinks readers should consult the original language.
The speaker now values wording that preserves the character's uncertainty.
answers: The speaker now values wording that preserves the character's uncertainty.

delivery.text: At first I preferred the earlier translation because the dialogue sounded smoother. The new version occasionally makes you pause over a phrase. Reading both more closely, I realised that those pauses occur where the character is struggling to say what she means. The older version gives her a confidence she does not have in the original. I still find the new one less comfortable to read, but I think that discomfort sometimes serves the story.

items.prompt: What is the speaker's concern about moving the club online?
options: It may weaken the informal contact that members value.
It may prevent members from hearing the main speaker.
It may cost more than renting the current hall.
It may make the formal programme too short.
answers: It may weaken the informal contact that members value.

delivery.text: Moving our monthly club meeting online would certainly save the hall fee, and I know some members would welcome avoiding the journey. My hesitation concerns the time before and after the talk. That is when new members introduce themselves and people arrange smaller activities. We could reproduce some of that online, but it would take planning. Keeping the lecture and dropping everything around it would preserve the timetable rather than the whole experience.

items.prompt: What distinction is central to the writer's criticism?
options: Written submissions versus face-to-face meetings.
Public consultation versus unanimous agreement.
The cost of consultation versus its duration.
Participation volume versus demonstrable influence on decisions.
answers: Participation volume versus demonstrable influence on decisions.
items.context: The committee describes its consultation as extensive, citing hundreds of written submissions. Quantity, however, tells us little about whose concerns shaped the final proposal. A transparent account would distinguish suggestions incorporated into the design from those considered and rejected, and explain the latter decisions. This would not require accepting every demand. It would allow participants to judge whether consultation informed a decision or merely accompanied one already taken. Without that account, the headline participation figure is an incomplete measure of the process's value.

items.prompt: What made the original analysis inadequate?
options: It gave complaints more weight than usage data from the start.
It showed that accessibility settings should never be evaluated.
It measured frequency without considering the consequences for dependent users.
Its usage counts were necessarily inaccurate.
answers: It measured frequency without considering the consequences for dependent users.
items.context: A product team removed a rarely used accessibility setting after a usage study. The aggregate figures seemed decisive, yet they concealed dependence: the few people using the setting relied on it to complete essential tasks. When complaints arrived, the team initially interpreted them as resistance to change. Reinstating the feature required little development time; understanding why the original analysis had misled them took longer. The episode illustrates how a sound count can support a poor decision when the question being counted is too narrow.

items.prompt: How does the display seek to maintain authority?
options: By avoiding any statement about objects with uncertain origins.
By showing the evidence and limits behind its claims.
By presenting every interpretation as equally supported.
By replacing historical records with visitors' opinions.
answers: By showing the evidence and limits behind its claims.
items.context: The museum's new display acknowledges uncertainty about the origins of several objects. Some trustees feared that this would undermine authority. Instead, the accompanying notes distinguish established records from plausible inferences and identify gaps that further research might address. Visitors are invited to see how knowledge is assembled, rather than simply being asked to trust an institutional voice. The approach risks appearing less definitive, but that risk is deliberate: authority here rests on making the basis of a claim inspectable.

items.prompt: What qualification does the writer add to the idea of reversibility?
options: Undoing a rule may leave consequences that cannot readily be undone.
A policy is reversible whenever its wording can be deleted.
Reversible policies never justify limited trials.
Caution is necessary only when a rule is permanent.
answers: Undoing a rule may leave consequences that cannot readily be undone.
items.context: An editorial praises a policy for being reversible, as though reversibility removed the need for caution. Yet a formal right to undo a decision is not the same as a practical ability to restore what preceded it. A trial may alter expectations, displace staff or cause records to be lost. These effects can persist after the rule itself is withdrawn. Reversibility remains a useful design aim, but it should be specified in terms of recoverable consequences rather than treated as a reassuring label.

items.prompt: What is the reviewer's attitude towards the pianist's changes?
options: They are justified mainly because the audience recognised them.
They are an impressive display that distracts from a weak composition.
They reveal possibilities in the music, despite initially seeming excessive.
They are acceptable as an experiment but unsuitable for the concert.
answers: They reveal possibilities in the music, despite initially seeming excessive.

delivery.text: In the opening movement, I wondered whether the pianist was determined to make every familiar phrase sound unfamiliar. The pauses seemed almost wilful. Yet by the finale, those interruptions had begun to make sense: themes that usually glide past had acquired an awkwardness, even a vulnerability, I had not heard before. I would not want every performance to follow her example. That would turn an interpretation into a mannerism. But this one earned its departures from convention, and the long silence before the applause felt appropriate.

items.prompt: What point is the editor making about effortless prose?
options: It may depend on extensive work that the finished text conceals.
It is best preserved by limiting the editor's involvement.
It usually emerges when an author keeps the first draft intact.
It is less suitable than visibly complex writing for serious subjects.
answers: It may depend on extensive work that the finished text conceals.

delivery.text: People describe her essays as conversational, as if she had merely thought aloud and sent the recording to a printer. Having edited three of them, I can say that the apparent ease is painstakingly made. We once spent an afternoon moving a single sentence, not because it was unclear, but because its position changed how the whole argument unfolded. None of that labour should be visible to the reader. The mistake is to assume that, because the writing asks little effort of us, it asked little of her.

items.prompt: What does the speaker imply about the proposed restoration?
options: Matching the oldest surviving photograph is the least subjective choice.
Leaving the garden untouched would preserve its intended design.
The residents' memories provide a more precise plan than the archives.
Choosing a historical version also means choosing what later history to remove.
answers: Choosing a historical version also means choosing what later history to remove.

delivery.text: The proposal is to restore the garden to its original design. The phrase sounds reassuringly precise, until you ask which original they mean. The first plan was altered before the planting was finished; the photograph everyone quotes was taken twenty years later. And the trees residents now associate with the place were added later still. A restoration could be worthwhile, but it would be an interpretation of the garden's history, not a neutral act of turning back the clock. We ought to be candid about what we would lose as well as what we hope to recover.

items.prompt: How does the speaker explain the value of the apprenticeship?
options: It replaced formal instruction with the freedom to make mistakes alone.
It developed judgment through guided exposure to ordinary decisions.
It provided a set of rules that could be applied without discussion.
It accelerated training by keeping beginners away from routine work.
answers: It developed judgment through guided exposure to ordinary decisions.

delivery.text: What I learned from the apprenticeship rarely arrived in the form of a lesson. I would watch my supervisor reject a piece that looked perfectly serviceable, then ask why. Sometimes the explanation concerned a flaw I could learn to spot; sometimes it concerned what a particular customer would notice or tolerate. This was not an argument against technical instruction. It was instruction in recognising when a rule settles the matter and when you need a more situated judgment. Without the questions and explanations, merely standing beside an expert would have taught me far less.
